title: Square Cover
context: Grade 5, the first area pages and the squared-paper activity. An adult sees counting. What the pages are doing is naming a new measure: the area is the amount of surface a figure covers, counted in unit squares, and it is kept apart from the perimeter, the length of the boundary.

writeup.why: Tell area, the surface a figure covers, from perimeter, the length of its boundary; pick the unit square that fits; count unit squares by rows; and compare areas only in squares of one size.
writeup.look: A figure on plain paper with a tray of violet unit squares under it, a string for the edge, a unit shelf on the second phase and two patches side by side on the last.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Square Cover' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of unit squares laid. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The figure lies at x 120, y 230 inside a box 620 by 360, drawn to one scale, its given sides labelled deep blue. The tray of violet unit squares, each labelled Unit square, runs along y 640 from x 120. The Lay a row button stands at x 800, y 250. The string, when laid, runs once round the figure's edge in vermilion, labelled Boundary, with its length written in ink beside the top edge. On the second phase the unit shelf stands at x 800, y 330 with three squares labelled by their sides, and the picture card sits at x 120, y 230. On the fourth phase Patch A stands at x 120, y 250 and Patch B at x 480, y 250, each with a counter under it, and the Bigger squares switch sits at x 800, y 420. The area reached is green. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with sq. cm, sq. m and sq. km keys. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the ten tools of this chapter share them. The lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, labelled Given or by their own name. The perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green, labelled Answer. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion, labelled Boundary. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet, labelled Unit square, Unit cube, Row or Layer. The part squares of an estimate and the space left over where no whole cube fits are rose, labelled More than half, Half or Left over. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, and nothing on this stage is ever grey. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its near-black outline, grid lines, unit words and signs are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last figure stays covered in violet squares with the string round its edge, and the area in green with its square unit.

writeup.delight: On the third phase, when the last row settles into place, the covered rectangle gives one soft ripple from corner to corner, like a tiled floor being finished.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet laid. On the first phase a card lies on the paper with a string coiled beside it and the tray of squares below. On the second the unit shelf stands beside a picture card of a surface. On the third an empty rectangle waits with the Lay a row button. On the fourth two patches stand side by side, uncounted. One thing moves, once: the tray, the unit shelf or the Lay a row button gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any rectangle along the grid, covered square by square or row by row, with the string round its edge. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on area and perimeter, units of area, counting by rows and comparing counts.

source_tool.description: A figure is drawn to one scale on plain paper, its given sides labelled deep blue. A tray of unit squares, each labelled Unit square and filled violet, sits under the working area. The child drags squares onto the figure one at a time, or taps Lay a row to lay a whole row along the length; squares snap edge to edge, and a square dropped over another or leaving a gap is drawn where it was dropped. A string can be laid once round the edge, lighting the boundary vermilion, labelled Boundary, with its length written beside it. A unit shelf holds three squares with sides of 1 cm, 1 m and 1 km, drawn as labels rather than to scale, and a picture card shows the surface to be measured. On the last phase two patches stand side by side with a counter under each, and one patch can be made of bigger squares. A number pad types a count or an area with sq. cm, sq. m and sq. km keys. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of squares laid.

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: squared paper with equal square cells, rulers marked in centimetres, unit cubes that stack into rows, layers and cuboids, open boxes, and clear jars of water with a level line.
Every figure is drawn to one scale inside its stage, so a side twice as long looks twice as long, and every square cell and every unit cube in one picture is the same size.
Every side, edge and measure carries its unit: cm or m for a length, sq. cm or sq. m for an area, and cu. cm or cu. m for a volume. The longer side of a rectangle is always the one labelled length.
A cuboid is drawn in three visible faces, and a cube only when all its edges are equal. Cubes hidden behind or under others are shown by a see-through layer when they are counted.
A part square on an estimate is marked by its kind, more than half, half or less than half, in words; no cross ever marks a square that is counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a walker tracing a boundary, rows of squares filling a rectangle, layers of cubes stacking into a cuboid, or water rising in a jar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a square, a cube or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, and the perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet. The part squares an area estimate rounds, and the space left over where no whole cube fits, are rose. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open and is not used here. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its outline, and grid lines and unit words are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Boundary, Unit square, Unit cube, Layer, More than half, Half and Left over, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

voice.onNext: A new surface. Cover it row by row.
voice.opening: A shape, a string and a tray of squares.
voice.onFinish: You measured a surface by the squares that cover it.

placement.where: After the class has covered a notebook with paper squares of one size, edge to edge, and counted them. The tool is what lays squares row by row beside a string round the same edge, so the two measures sit side by side.

answer_key.rule: The area of a figure is the amount of surface it covers. A square with sides of 1 cm is a unit square, with an area of 1 sq. cm; area is measured in square units, sq. cm for small surfaces, sq. m for large ones and sq. km for very large ones. The number of unit squares that cover a surface, with no gaps and no overlaps, is its area; count them by rows. Two areas can be compared by counting only when the squares are the same size. A perimeter is the length of the boundary, a length in cm or m.
answer_key.wrong: The squares the child laid stay where they are, and the stage lays a ghost row beside them to show the gap, the overlap or the row left out, lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The string lies along the boundary, so its length is the perimeter: 16 cm.
The squares cover the surface inside, so their count is the area: 15 sq. cm.
A perimeter is a length in cm, and an area is a surface in sq. cm.
items.answer: The area is 15 sq. cm and the perimeter is 16 cm
items.question: A card is covered by 15 unit squares of side 1 cm, and a string laid once round its edge is 16 cm long. Which number gives its area, and which gives its perimeter?
items.checkpoint: The string measures the edge; the squares measure the surface.
items.misconception: Calling the length of the string the area, because both numbers describe the same card.

steps: A unit square with sides of 1 cm is 1 sq. cm, about the size of a fingertip.
A unit square with sides of 1 m is 1 sq. m, about the size of a small mat.
A playground is a large surface, but far smaller than a city, so sq. m fits.
items.question: Which unit fits the area of a school playground: sq. cm, sq. m or sq. km?
items.checkpoint: Small surfaces use sq. cm, large ones sq. m and very large ones sq. km.
items.misconception: Choosing sq. km because a playground feels big, though sq. km is for a city or a state.

steps: Lay the squares in rows along the length: 9 squares in each row.
There are 4 rows, one for each cm of the breadth.
So the area of a 9 cm by 4 cm rectangle is 36 sq. cm.
items.question: A rectangle 9 cm long and 4 cm wide is covered with 1 cm squares. How many squares cover it, and what is its area?
items.checkpoint: Count by rows: every row has the same number of squares.
items.misconception: Counting only the squares along the edge, which gives a ring round the boundary, not the whole surface.

steps: The counts can be compared because all the squares are the same size.
items.question: Patch A is 10 squares by 2 squares. Patch B is 7 squares by 3 squares. All the squares are the same size. Which patch covers more?
items.checkpoint: Compare counts only when the squares are the same size.
items.misconception: Choosing Patch A because it is longer, though a longer patch can cover less.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Does a fence round a garden measure its perimeter or its area?
items.final_answer: Its perimeter, the length of the boundary

items.question: What is the area of one unit square with sides of 1 m?
A rectangle is 8 cm long and 2 cm wide. How many 1 cm squares cover it?
Which unit fits the area of a postage stamp: sq. cm, sq. m or sq. km?
A rectangle 13 cm long and 3 cm wide is covered with 1 cm squares. What is its area?
Patch A is 9 squares by 3 squares. Patch B is 6 squares by 4 squares. The squares are the same size. Which covers more?
items.final_answer: Patch A covers 27 squares and Patch B covers 24, so Patch A covers more

items.question: One patch is covered by 20 small squares and another by 12 big squares. Can the counts alone say which covers more?
items.final_answer: No. Counts can be compared only when the squares are the same size

items.question: A rectangle 14 cm long and 5 cm wide is covered with 1 cm squares. What is its area?
items.final_answer: 5 rows of 14: 14 + 14 + 14 + 14 + 14 = 70, so the area of a 14 cm by 5 cm rectangle is 70 sq. cm

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

teaching_notes: Cover a book with paper squares of one size before the tool opens, and count them. Keep the two measures apart from the first minute: the string measures the length of the boundary and the squares measure the surface. Say the unit every time, sq. cm for a book and sq. m for a floor. Count by rows, the same number in every row, and lay the rows along the longer side, the length. Compare two areas by counting only when the squares are the same size. The printed rectangles and figures are the child's to count.
